topic: International Trade and the Global Economy
subject: economics

items.title: US tariffs on China were largely absorbed by US importers
items.claim: Amiti, Redding and Weinstein (Journal of Economic Perspectives, 2019) studied the incidence of 2018 US tariffs on Chinese imports. What did they find?

options.text: Chinese exporters paid the entire tariff
Nearly the full cost of the tariffs was passed through to US importers and consumers; producer prices in China barely changed. The 'tariffs hurt foreigners' framing did not match the price data

items.reveal:
Amiti, Redding and Weinstein analysed customs and price data through 2019. The pass-through was nearly complete to US importers; Chinese export prices for affected goods didn't drop substantially.

Fajgelbaum, Goldberg, Kennedy and Khandelwal (QJE 2020) confirmed the finding using different methods. Subsequent Biden-era tariffs (2024) followed similar patterns. The US-China tariffs reshaped supply chains (Vietnam, Mexico saw substantial increases in exports to the US) more than they raised significant revenue.
items.why: The political rhetoric of tariffs often diverges from the economic incidence. Trade policy effects are empirically measurable; the empirics often don't support the political framing.

items.title: Fiscal multipliers are larger in recessions
items.claim: The IMF's 2012 World Economic Outlook (Blanchard and Leigh) revised fiscal multiplier estimates upward, particularly for recessions. What was the policy implication?

options.text: Fiscal consolidation in 2010-12 reduced GDP more than initial IMF forecasts assumed (multiplier of ~0.5 in normal times rose to ~1.5+ at the ZLB); contributed to slower recovery, especially in eurozone periphery
Fiscal policy has no effect on GDP

items.reveal:
Blanchard and Leigh's IMF Working Paper 13/1 acknowledged that the IMF and others had underestimated multipliers in the post-2008 environment. Reinhart-Rogoff's debt-threshold claims also influenced austerity policies that contributed to UK and Eurozone double-dips.

Research since (Auerbach & Gorodnichenko 2012, Ramey 2019) shows multipliers vary with the state of the economy — generally larger in recessions, smaller in expansions or when monetary policy can offset fiscal contraction.
items.why: A single 'multiplier' number hides important variation. The same fiscal policy can have very different effects in different macroeconomic states.

items.title: Network effects can produce winner-take-all markets
items.claim: A product becomes more valuable to each user as more users join (telephone, social networks, payment platforms). What does this often produce?

options.text: Strong tendencies to concentration: 'winner-take-all' or 'winner-take-most' markets, often with one or two dominant firms; antitrust intervention becomes harder because consumer prices may be low while market power is high

items.reveal:
Direct network effects: more users → more value (Facebook, WhatsApp). Indirect (cross-side): more buyers attract more sellers and vice versa (Uber, marketplaces).

W. Brian Arthur's 1989 paper on increasing returns formalised the dynamics. Modern antitrust debate (Lina Khan's 2017 'Amazon's Antitrust Paradox') argues consumer-welfare frameworks miss platform power. EU Digital Markets Act (2022) and US recent FTC actions reflect this view.
items.why: Digital markets often don't fit the perfectly-competitive framework of textbook microeconomics. Regulators have had to develop new approaches as a result.
